clue.text: Blooms set up in a jumble

indicators.note: a jumble is a disordered heap, so the preceding letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Flowers have been arranged in an untidy heap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' looks like part of the picture of arranging flowers, but its letters are raw material, along with 'in a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Petunias are popular garden flowers, so they are an example of blooms.

clue.text: Give satisfaction, if you'd be so kind

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, to delight or content someone
second meaning: the polite word attached to a request

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one polite request; it is really two separate meanings of one word, a verb and a courtesy.
explanation.definitionFit: To content someone is to do this verb, and the same word is the standard polite marker added when asking a favour.

clue.text: Tory, in vain, regularly advanced minutiae

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters of these words
A is the abbreviation for advanced, as in A level

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician has vainly been pushing small, fussy details.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make 'in vain' an aside about the Tory, but the words are just a source of every second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Minutiae are small, unimportant details, which is a close synonym of trifling facts and particulars.

clue.text: Losing unfurled umbrella, Simon Russell Beale unusually quiet

indicators.note: losing something means it is taken away, so letters are removed
unusually means not in the normal way, so the remaining letters take an unusual order

blocks.note: the actor's full name taken as written
the letters to take away; unfurled means they are removed wherever they sit, not as a block

explanation.surface: The actor Simon Russell Beale, without his opened umbrella, is strangely silent.
explanation.walkthrough: Strike the eight letters of UMBRELLA from the actor's name, wherever they fall, leaving SIONSSELE, which rearranges to NOISELESS. Simon Russell Beale is a celebrated English stage actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Something noiseless makes no sound at all, so it is a direct synonym of quiet as an adjective.

clue.text: Seas that Armada tours, going round the bend

indicators.note: touring means wandering around rather than going straight, so the letters wander into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The Spanish Armada sails the seas, rounding a bend in the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going round the bend' sounds like more sailing, but it is the definition: British slang for going mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Going round the bend is a British idiom for losing one's sanity, and the simile describes someone completely crazy.

clue.text: Computer in flipping pocket, mate

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters are turned back to front

blocks.note: to pocket a ball in snooker is to pot it
a pal is a friend or mate

explanation.surface: Someone exasperatedly tells a friend the computer is in their blasted pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British curse, but it is the reversal signal; 'pocket' is a verb, as in snooker.
explanation.definitionFit: A laptop is a portable personal computer, so it is a specific example of the general term.

clue.text: Extract from reggae's oppressed storyteller

indicators.note: an extract is a piece taken out of something longer, so the letters sit inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the apostrophe and into the next word

explanation.surface: A quoted passage from a reggae song about an oppressed narrator.
explanation.walkthrough: Reggae lyrics often tell of oppression, which makes the surface convincing; the apostrophe is ignored when reading the letters through.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek teller of fables, the most famous storyteller of moral animal tales.

clue.text: 'The REM Introduction' begins with eerie instrument

indicators.note: the title's opening run of letters is what is wanted, so the answer sits at its start

blocks.note: the first eight letters of this made-up title, read straight through

explanation.surface: An album or documentary about the band R.E.M. opens with a spooky musical sound.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitalised title suggests the rock band, but read the letters without spaces and the instrument appears at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The theremin is an electronic instrument played without touch, famous for the wavering spooky sound in old science-fiction films.

clue.text: Assuming Post Office finding location

blocks.note: PO is the standard abbreviation
siting is choosing the place where something will go

explanation.surface: Someone guesses where the post office is to be found.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assuming' looks like a link word setting up a supposition; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To posit is to put forward as a basis for argument, so positing means taking something as given.

clue.text: Toppling Trojan King: to me, it's a serious business

indicators.note: something toppling falls over and lands in disarray, so the letters land in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone declares that bringing down the King of Troy is grave work.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon seems to introduce a speaker's verdict, but 'to me' is part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is no joking matter must be treated gravely, the idiomatic equivalent of a serious affair.

clue.text: Partially candlelit? Is mum displaying snobbery?

indicators.note: partially means only in part, so only a part of the following words is used

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words, ignoring the punctuation

explanation.surface: Mother insists on candlelight at dinner, and someone wonders whether she is being a snob.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark breaks the run of letters on the surface, but the answer reads straight through it.
explanation.definitionFit: Elitism is the belief that a select few are superior, which is the attitude behind snobbery.

clue.text: Yes, sort out seafood

indicators.note: sorting something out means rearranging it into order, so the letters are reorganised

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, doubling as part of the indicator

explanation.surface: Someone agrees to deal with the fish order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort' does double duty: its letters join YES, and together with 'out' it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Oysters are shellfish eaten as a delicacy, so they are an example of the broader category.

clue.text: Take possession of oceans, by sound of it

indicators.note: judging by how it sounds means we hear a word rather than read it

blocks.note: oceans are seas, and the plural is said the same as the verb

explanation.surface: Someone claims ownership of the oceans, a grand naval ambition.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests seizing the seas themselves; only the sound of the plural noun matters.
explanation.definitionFit: To seize something is to grab it and take control, a direct synonym of taking possession.

clue.text: Dutch grub includes pies most feeble

indicators.note: to include is to take inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for Dutch
to grub about is to root around, digging for something
taken as written

explanation.surface: Food from the Netherlands contains some really weak pies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub' looks like a noun for food, which fits the pies; here it is a verb, meaning to dig about.
explanation.definitionFit: Something droopy sags limply, lacking vigour, so the superlative describes the weakest and least spirited.

clue.text: For each spirit, a bubbly knocked back: no sweat

indicators.note: something bubbly is fizzing and agitated, so the letters are stirred up
knocking something back sends it backwards, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: per means for each, as in per person
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Drinking a spirit and some fizz with every round is no strain at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bubbly' and 'knocked back' both suggest drinking champagne, but they are instructions. 'No sweat' seems a single idiom; 'sweat' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Perspiration is the moisture the skin releases when hot, the formal word for the same bodily fluid.

clue.text: Love pretentiousness? No thanks

indicators.note: saying no to something means doing without it, so letters are dropped

blocks.note: affectation is putting on airs, behaviour meant to impress
ta is informal British for thank you

explanation.surface: Someone is offered pretentious love and politely declines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No thanks' reads as a polite refusal; it tells you to remove the British word for thanks from the longer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Affection is a feeling of fondness and warmth, a gentle synonym of love as a noun.

clue.text: Muscle vacuous: dangerous second prisoner held, escapes

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word is emptied of its inside and only its ends stay
to be held is to be gripped from both sides, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: an ab is an abdominal muscle
the first and last letters only
S is the abbreviation for second
a con is a convict

explanation.surface: A dangerous but empty-headed muscleman, the second inmate held, breaks out of jail.
explanation.walkthrough: The second and the prisoner go together inside the outer pair, AB and the emptied 'dangerous'.
explanation.definitionFit: To abscond is to leave secretly to avoid arrest or duty, so absconds means runs off or gets away.

clue.text: Exasperated utterance, revolting slop he put before setter

indicators.note: revolting means rising up and overturning, so the letters are overturned into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the setter refers to themself as me

explanation.surface: Someone groans in frustration at the disgusting slop a man served the setter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' looks like a description of the slop, as in disgusting; it means overturning.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a cry of frustration or a mock oath, said when someone is pushed to the limit of patience.

clue.text: Discloses secret: distressed staff beg, howl

indicators.note: distressed means battered or agitated, so the letters are knocked about

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An informant reveals a secret while upset workers plead and wail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distressed' fits the begging, howling staff so well that it reads as plain description; it is the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Blowing the gaff is a British idiom for revealing a plot or secret, so it matches disclosing confidential information.

clue.text: Conks out, 'empty' sign, learner driver wanting fuel

blocks.note: an engine that conks out dies
E marks empty on a fuel gauge
L is the learner plate on a car in Britain

explanation.surface: A learner's car breaks down with the gauge on empty because they need petrol.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface is a breakdown story; 'wanting' only joins wordplay to definition. British learner drivers display an L plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Diesel is a heavy oil burned in compression-ignition engines, a common type of vehicle fuel.

clue.text: University official: 'Everyman's wearing, lower in reputation'

indicators.note: something being worn is wrapped around by the wearer, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a dean heads a faculty or college
Everyman is the setter, who refers to themself as me; the 's means 'is'

explanation.surface: A university official says the setter's clothing is hurting his standing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Everyman's' reads as a possessive, but it is 'Everyman is', the setter being worn by the official.
explanation.definitionFit: To demean someone is to degrade them and reduce their dignity or the respect others have for them.

clue.text: Queen, King in palace to broadcast

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter widely, so the letters are scattered into a new arrangement

blocks.note: R is short for rex, Latin for king
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A queen and king make a televised address from their palace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' only places the king among the letters; since everything is rearranged, where he sits does not matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleopatra was the last ruling queen of ancient Egypt, a famous example of a female monarch.

clue.text: Flop down, Chubby

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, to drop heavily into a seat
second meaning: an adjective, pleasantly rounded

explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'Chubby' look like someone being told to sit; the two halves are a verb and an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to sit down heavily and abruptly, and to be rounded and slightly fat.

clue.text: Report of distant country

indicators.note: a report is a sound, as of a gun, so we listen for a word rather than read it

blocks.note: distant in manner is cool or unfriendly

explanation.surface: A news report from some far-off land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distant country' reads as one phrase; 'distant' is in fact the wordplay, meaning aloof, and 'country' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Chile is a long, narrow South American nation on the Pacific coast, so it fits the definition directly.

clue.text: God, write about air

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to pen is to write
an air is a melody

explanation.surface: An instruction to compose something about a deity of the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' suggests the sky or atmosphere; here it is a melody, as in a song.
explanation.definitionFit: Neptune is the Roman god of the sea, so he is one of the classical deities.

clue.text: Sad in France, English staying in seaside city

indicators.note: something staying in a place lodges inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: triste is the French word for sad
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An English tourist feels gloomy in France while on holiday in a coastal town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In France' looks like a location in the story; it says the word for sad is French.
explanation.definitionFit: Trieste is a port city in north-eastern Italy on the Adriatic coast, so it is a city by the sea.

clue.text: Son getting spa treatments lies back, rests

indicators.note: lying back means reclining backwards, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
a peel is a skin treatment at a spa

explanation.surface: A son at a spa reclines and relaxes while being pampered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lies back' and 'rests' sound like one lazy scene; the first phrase turns the son and treatments around.
explanation.definitionFit: To sleep is to rest in a state of unconsciousness, so the verb forms match as near synonyms.

clue.text: A founding father who demanded respect?

blocks.note: first meaning: Benjamin, a signatory of the American Declaration of Independence
second meaning: Aretha, the soul singer whose hit song spelt out the word R-E-S-P-E-C-T

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one stern patriarch; the question mark warns that the second half is Aretha's signature hit 'Respect'.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin of this surname helped found the United States, and Aretha of the same surname famously sang a demand for respect.
